title: The funeral
hook: eulogy, psalms, and the prayer "God full of mercy"

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was keriah, and your line was the tear: grief made visible. Whose grief did you let show without fixing it? Today the mourners, torn garments and all, walk into the funeral. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

No flowers on the plain wooden coffin. Folding chairs, a small chapel, people in coats they don't wear often. A grandson stands up, unfolds a sheet of paper, and tells a story about fishing that makes the whole room laugh and then go quiet. Someone reads a psalm. And then the cantor, or a rabbi, or a friend who knows the tune, begins to sing in Hebrew. It's slow, rising and falling, and in the middle of it comes a name: the name of the person in the coffin, sung out loud. Today's word is that song.
screen: `A PLAIN COFFIN, NO FLOWERS.` → `A STORY ABOUT FISHING.` → `A NAME, SUNG OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: El Male Rachamim. God full of mercy. Turn the funeral four ways. First, the eulogy, the hesped. When Sarah dies, Genesis says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her." The rabbis saw a eulogy there. A hesped is meant to do both: speak about the person, and let people weep. The codes ask the speaker to praise truly, not to invent a saint, because an honest picture honors the dead more than a flattering one. Second, the psalms. Psalms are read, and Psalm twenty-three may be among them: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." It is read as company for the road, not as an explanation. Third, the prayer. El Male Rachamim is a short memorial prayer, usually sung. It calls on God full of mercy, who dwells on high, to give true rest to the soul of the one who has died, beneath the wings of the divine presence, and it names them. It asks that their soul be bound up in the bond of life. It may be sung again at the grave, and later on days of remembrance. Fourth, the name. In the middle of that slow melody, one ordinary name, sung as if it belongs there. In that moment the funeral says, out loud and together, that this person mattered, and to hand them, by name, to mercy. God full of mercy.
screen: `THE HESPED: SPEAK TRULY.` · `THE LORD IS MY SHEPHERD.` · `REST BENEATH THE WINGS.` · `ONE NAME, SUNG.` · then, large: `GOD FULL OF MERCY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be present for someone grieving. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you know who is grieving now, or who lost someone this year. Breathe in, and see them in a crowded room after the service, with everyone saying the same few lines. Breathe out, and think what it would mean to simply sit beside them. No speech. Maybe the name of the person they lost, said gently, so they hear it again. If you pray, you can hold that name in your prayer, or sit in silence. The bell holds the time.
El Male Rachamim. God full of mercy: the sung memorial prayer that asks rest for the soul and says the person's name. Today's word.
Your line: god full of mercy. Today, say the name of someone who died, out loud, to someone who loved them too. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: A Jewish funeral is usually simple: a eulogy (hesped), psalms, and the memorial prayer El Male Rachamim, sung by a cantor or rabbi with the name of the person who died; it is often sung again at the graveside.

trapdoor: what you thought: El Male Rachamim is a general prayer for the dead.
what it means: a sung memorial prayer that asks rest for one soul, by name, beneath the wings of the divine presence.
what a scholar hears: its 'bond of life' echoes Abigail's words in 1 Samuel 25:29; the hesped is read from Genesis 23:2.

notes: Genesis 23:2 and Psalm 23:1 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm exact wording.

El Male Rachamim described, not quoted or translated in full: God full of mercy who dwells on high, true rest beneath the wings of the Shechinah, bound in the bond of life (1 Samuel 25:29). Confirm summary.
Shulchan Aruch YD 344 (eulogize truly; slight but not great exaggeration) paraphrased as 'praise truly, not invent a saint'; confirm.
'Psalm twenty-three is often among them' and 'sung again at the grave, and later on days of remembrance' kept general; confirm. Note: the index carry 'god full of mercy' is lowercase; kept exactly.
Genesis 23:2 read as the source of the hesped (Hebrew lispod): confirm the rabbinic reading.
No flowers at the funeral: customary in many communities; confirm.
